Why recurse?

Switching a crossing need not reduce the crossing count. Instead, we make the diagram descending: traverse each component and meet every crossing over-first. A descending diagram is an unlink.

Smoothing removes a crossing. Together, these two moves make the recursion terminate.

READING THE CALCULATION

From a diagram
to a polynomial.

1. Choose a crossing

Orient the link and choose an under-first crossing. The marked disk isolates the local change; everything outside it stays the same.

2. Switch and smooth

For a positive crossing, ∇ = ∇switch + z∇smooth. For a negative crossing, subtract the smoothed term. Smoothing reconnects incoming strands to the opposite outgoing strands, respecting orientation.

3. Reach the base cases

An unknot contributes 1. An unlink with two or more components contributes 0. Work back up the tree to combine the answers.

4. Change variables

Substitute z = t1/2 − t−1/2. For the cinquefoil, 1 + 3z² + z⁴ becomes t⁻² − t⁻¹ + 1 − t + t².

This tool computes an invariant, not a complete knot identification. Different knots can have the same Alexander polynomial. Drawing mode accepts one closed polygonal component; avoid tangencies, triple crossings, and crossings at vertices. Up to 12 crossings.
